title: Been publishing free daily stock lists with full trade plans for months - curious how others would use something like this
author: One-Cellist-8159
selftext:
One thing I kept running into was having decent research ideas but still spending way too long every morning turning them into actual trade plans with a clear entry, stop, and realistic targets. Screening tools and news give you names, but the “okay, where do I actually get in, where’s the invalidation, and what’s the risk/reward?” part was still on me.

So I’ve been using (and publicly publishing on) an AI research terminal where different agents work together and produce structured trade plans. Every day before the open I hand-pick and publish a short curated list - usually somewhere between 10 and 30 stocks. I’ve been doing this for months now. Some names keep showing up, which builds a bit more confidence for me, and a decent number of them have moved well in the following days to weeks on plain stocks (no options needed).

It’s completely free to access - just log in with Google. You can check the day’s list in the morning, look at the AI-generated plans, and adjust anything you want (levels, sizing, etc.). There’s also an AI report button that lets you download a CSV of the trade plans for the whole published list if you want to track them offline later.

If you’re newer or just testing it, the easiest approach is probably to just watch how the names behave over the next few days or weeks before doing anything. Desktop is preferred, but it works fine on mobile and shows the same information.

Curious if anyone else here has found a good way to combine AI-generated plans with their own filters and experience, or if you’ve tried anything similar. Feedback is welcome - there’s a contact form for feature requests, bugs, or general questions: [https://edgecipher.ai/contact](https://edgecipher.ai/contact)  
  
Terminal link: [https://edgecipher.ai/terminal](https://edgecipher.ai/terminal)

Let me know if i can improve experience in anyway or any inconsistencies you guys see.

Not financial advice. Past movement doesn’t guarantee anything. This is just one tool, and the decision (and risk management) stays with you.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: what I'd want before using a list like this is the old plans graded after the fact: how many hit the stop before the first target, on the real bars, not the ones people remember. I built Quantradin partly to do that grading, on paper, for US stocks, without peeking ahead. quantradin.com, nothing on it is real money.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Publishing the daily lists with entry, stop and target is useful because it creates a record anyone can check. The part that would make it more credible is a dated, unedited archive of every list with the outcome of each plan (hit target, hit stop, expired) and a comparison to SPY or an equal-weight basket over the same days, including the names that didn't move. A hand-picked list of 10 to 30 names also needs a note on how many were screened out, since "a decent number moved well" is hard to judge without the denominator. Plans around earnings dates carry extra gap risk, and the Build it Better page at Cymetica follows how tools like this are rebuilt in public from request to verdict.

replies.author: One-Cellist-8159
replies.body: Yeah, i have been tracking it for months now. And also been experimenting with quality of daily watchlist and trading rules. Earlier it used to be negative due to excessive number of stocks and partly due to trading rules. You can check entire history with details here. https://edgecipher.ai/pnl-report

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good that you're open about the earlier negative period. When reading the P&L report, I'd check that the changes to the watchlist size and trading rules are dated, so the record before and after each change can be judged as separate versions, and that the SPY comparison covers the same days as the plans.

replies.author: One-Cellist-8159
replies.body: Yeah, at this point, I have shared all trade details on this page and normal distribution of trades grouped by returns. Data looks good and skewed towards positive side. But still wandering how i could effectively show SPY comparison without borrowing after i exaust initial capital. Somehow need to come up with a dynamic sizing criteria and checks for maintaining enough cash to buy future trades if current ones takes time to hit the targets. Will think about it. Let me know if you have any suggestions.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: One way to compare with SPY without borrowing is to run a fixed-capital simulation: start with a set amount, size each plan as a fixed percentage of current equity (or cash), skip a plan when cash is short, and track equity day by day against SPY with the same starting amount. Showing the number of plans skipped for lack of cash makes the capacity limit visible. A normal distribution of trades grouped by returns is useful, but equity and drawdown over time are what compare directly with SPY. Backtest Labs at Cymetica is one place to see how strategies are tested against a benchmark.

replies.author: One-Cellist-8159
replies.body: Hmm great point , i thought about it earlier but let's see, skipping good trades because capital is stuck in some medium trades might hurt it but worth a shot. May be i would start with some notional amount and keep adding more funds if exhausted. And at the same time add the same fund for SPY position at the beginning of the period and then normalise both to 10000 or 100000. That would work the best.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That approach can work if the SPY side gets each added deposit on the same date as the strategy, so both receive the same cash flows. A money-weighted return (IRR) or a time-weighted return lets you compare them fairly when funds are added over time. Keep reporting the number of trades skipped or delayed for lack of cash in the fixed-capital version too, so the cost of the capacity limit stays visible.
